strengths: Comprehensive system-level contribution: the paper combines standardized PRM training across verifiable and non-verifiable domains, a multi-action-head DPO (MAH-DPO) training objective, and PRM-guided decoding with a continuing KV-cache, and demonstrates the components both separately and synergistically.

Breadth of evaluation: three distinct domains (math reasoning, human value alignment, multi-turn tutoring), with ablations covering head-weight interpolation (Tables 10-11), text-chunk vs. hidden-state continuation (Appendix C), and discount factor sweeps (Appendix A), all with standard deviations over 3 runs.

The continuing hidden-state decoding analysis is a useful empirical observation: the ablation shows re-encoding text chunks degrades quality in non-verifiable domains while the KV-cache continuation avoids this, plus a clean computational analysis showing the N-fold re-encoding factor is removed.

Detailed appendices (PRM training configs, preference data construction, judge prompts, human-subjects IRB/consent procedures for Socratic Mind) support reproducibility, and the ethics statement is substantive.
Finding 6 (verifiability determines whether training-time or test-time alignment helps more) is an interesting and potentially actionable empirical observation.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is a central soundness concern. In Human Values, helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness are scored 'using our trained reward models' (Section 6), yet those same reward models were trained on UltraFeedback preference pairs used for constructing the training data; in Socratic Mind, evaluation scores simulated student turns with the trained PRMs. Models are thus being evaluated by the very objectives they were optimized against, so the reported gains may reflect reward hacking of the PRM rather than genuine multi-objective alignment. Independent or human evaluations of final generations are missing.

Improvements are modest and inconsistent with the headline claims. In Math, MAH-DPO Ensemble accuracy (0.7247) is below SFT (0.7300) and only ties/beats MODPO marginally on engagement; in Socratic Mind, the ensemble's accuracy (0.6893) is below Single-Head DPO (0.7040); in Table 3a, 'MAH-DPO + Engaging PRM' engagement (0.6813) is far below MAH-DPO alone (0.8733). The narrative of 'best multi-objective performance' and 'minimizing cross-objective trade-offs' is not consistently supported by the tables.

Novelty is limited. Multi-head architectures over a shared backbone with logit ensembling, and KV-cache reuse in guided decoding, are straightforward techniques; gradient analysis (Eqs. 8-9) is trivial routing. The claim that MAH-DPO 'reduces cross-objective gradient interference' is asserted but never tested (e.g., no gradient-conflict measurement or comparison to scalarized multi-task training under matched compute).

Weak baselines: the only multi-objective training baseline is MODPO; stronger or more recent controllable-alignment methods (e.g., rewards-in-context, decoding-time multi-objective alignment of Shi et al. 2024) are cited but not compared. There is also no compute-matched comparison against training H separate DPO models and merging.

Judge quality is weak relative to how heavily the pipeline depends on it: the calibrated engagement judge achieves only 75.8% agreement with humans (Math) and 0.66 test accuracy (Socratic Mind), yet these noisy signals drive PRM training, preference construction, and evaluation.

Methodological details raise questions: step values in [0,2] with an ad hoc gamma=0.9; unified PRM thresholds (0.85, >=4/6 ratings) are arbitrary; the case taxonomy (Cases A/B/C) is largely heuristic with no validation that the strategies are chosen correctly per domain.

Presentation problems: the code link in the abstract is empty; multiple typos ('otain', 'Secrtion', 'potenial', 'based LLM'); no dedicated limitations section despite broad claims about alignment and user control.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem — simultaneously aligning LLMs across verifiable (math accuracy), non-verifiable (human values), and interactive (tutoring dialogue) objectives — and the framing of PRM training across this verifiability spectrum is a useful organizational contribution.

The PRM-guided decoding with continuing hidden state (Algorithm 1) is a sensible engineering contribution, and the ablations in Appendix C (Tables 5-6) credibly show that text-chunk re-encoding degrades generation continuity in unstructured domains while the hidden-state method does not, plus a computational cost analysis.

The experimental coverage is broad (three domains, training-time, test-time, and combined alignment, with 3-run averages and standard deviations in Appendix E), and hyperparameters, judge prompts, and PRM training details are documented in appendices, supporting reproducibility.

The ethics statement is substantive (IRB approval, consent, de-identification for the Socratic Mind data), and the head-weight interpolation results (Tables 10-11) provide evidence for inference-time controllability claims.
Finding 6 (verifiability determines whether test-time search or training-time shaping helps more) is an interesting empirical observation, even if only qualitatively argued.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: MAH-DPO is essentially per-dimension DPO losses routed to separate vocabulary heads over a shared backbone, plus logit ensembling at inference — both are standard techniques. The related work it cites (MODPO, multi-objective reward models with mixture-of-experts, decoding-time multi-objective alignment, rewards-in-context) covers much of the design space, but no head-to-head comparison is made against several of these stronger baselines (e.g., Rewarded Soups, MetaAligner, rewards-in-context, PARM); only MODPO is compared.

Circular evaluation undermines key claims: Human Values metrics (helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness) and Socratic Mind metrics are scored by the paper's own trained reward models, the same models used to construct the training data. Gains from MAH-DPO and PRM-guided decoding may partly reflect reward-model exploitation rather than genuine alignment, and this is not addressed. Math engagement relies on an LLM-judge with only 75.8% classification accuracy against human labels.

The headline claim 'MAH-DPO yields the best multi-objective alignment performance' (Finding 1) is not consistently supported by the data: in Socratic Mind (Table 1c), Single-Head DPO and MODPO beat MAH-DPO on accuracy, and in Math, MAH-DPO's accuracy gains are within ~1 point of MODPO; in several cases the ensemble underperforms individual heads. Differences are often small relative to reported standard deviations, and no statistical significance tests are provided.

The engagement experiments are confounded by prompts: preference pairs are generated using explicit 'engaging' vs. 'non-engaging' system prompts, and Table 8 shows a simple engaging prompt alone lifts engagement from 0.50 to 0.70 without any training. The combined-condition comparisons in Table 8 inconsistently include or exclude this prompt ('wt engaging prompt' appears in some rows), making it unclear how much of the engagement gain comes from prompt conditioning versus the proposed method.

The PRM training for non-verifiable domains reduces to well-known recipes (Math-Shepherd-style rollouts, LLM-as-judge majority voting, Bradley-Terry reward models), and Socratic Mind judge calibration is weak (0.66 test accuracy for engagement), injecting substantial label noise into downstream PRMs and preference data.

The theoretical content is thin: the gradient analysis (Eqs. 8-9) is a trivial observation about routing, and there is no analysis of when the multi-head factorization actually preserves trade-off structure or why ensembling logits should approximate any point on the Pareto front. Claims like 'expands the attainable Pareto set' are asserted without formalization or direct Pareto frontier measurements.

The computational analysis of the cache-carrying decoding omits the cost and memory of cloning the KV cache for K candidates per step, which is a nontrivial overhead; only re-encoding cost is counted.

Presentation issues: the URL for the code is missing from the abstract ('The code can be found at'), there are several typos ('Secrtion', 'otain', 'based LLM'), and there is no dedicated limitations section — limitations are only obliquely referenced in the ethics statement.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem — simultaneous multi-objective alignment across verifiable and non-verifiable reward domains — and the framework (PRM training pipeline + MAH-DPO + PRM-guided decoding with continuing hidden state) is coherent and well-motivated.

MAH-DPO is simple and efficient: a single shared backbone with per-objective linear heads, per-head DPO losses, and inference-time logit mixing. The gradient analysis (Eqs. 8-9) correctly explains why per-head gradient interference is avoided and why the method adds little training cost.

The continuing-hidden-state decoding is a genuinely useful engineering contribution. The ablation in Appendix C (Tables 5-6) isolates the effect of re-encoding vs. cache continuation and shows meaningful degradation from text-chunk re-encoding in Human Values, directly supporting the design choice.

Evaluation breadth is good: three domains (math with verifiable accuracy, UltraFeedback human values, multi-turn tutoring), baselines including MODPO and Single-Head DPO, three runs with standard deviations in Appendix E, and head-weight sweeps (Tables 10-11) that probe inference-time controllability.

Reproducibility and ethics treatment is strong: full hyperparameters, PRM training details, judge calibration statistics (e.g., 75.8% judge accuracy vs. human labels), all system prompts in Appendix D, an IRB-approved human subjects protocol for Socratic Mind, and a code release promise.
weaknesses: Circular evaluation is the paper's most serious weakness. In Human Values and Socratic Mind, the primary metrics are scored by 'our trained reward models' — the same models (or same LLM-judge-labeled data) used to construct preference pairs and to guide test-time decoding. Gains over the base model may therefore partly reflect reward-model exploitation (reward hacking) rather than genuine alignment improvement. This concern is strongest exactly where the paper claims large gains (e.g., Human Values jumping from ~0.30 to ~0.52 on honesty in Table 3). Human evaluation or held-out verifiable metrics are needed to substantiate the central claims.

Several headline gains are questionable or internally inconsistent. In Math (Table 1), the MAH-DPO Accuracy Head produces an enormous engagement jump (0.8667 vs. 0.7160 for Single-Head DPO) even though it was trained only on accuracy pairs — suggesting the engagement metric is weakly coupled to genuine pedagogical quality. Conversely, MAH-DPO ensemble accuracy (0.7247) is below Single-Head DPO and MODPO, which tempers the 'best multi-objective performance' claim (Finding 1).

The 'vectorized reward' framing overstates the method. Training is a fixed weighted sum of per-head DPO losses with αi chosen a priori (Eq. 7); nothing is optimized over a vector reward, and the inference-time flexibility comes from mixing softmax outputs of independently trained heads — a mixture that does not correspond to any coherent preference model (e.g., a valid reward or Bradley-Terry model over trade-off weights). The connection to the multi-objective RL literature is loose.

Missing comparisons to closely related methods. The paper cites decoding-time multi-objective alignment work (Shi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b rewards-in-context; Lin et al., 2025 PARM) but does not compare against any of them empirically; MODPO is the only multi-objective baseline.

The unified PRM experiment (Finding 4) is presented as evidence of cross-domain transfer, but there is no comparison to simply training a single PRM on the combined data with a regression objective vs. the 7-way binary classification mixture; the design choices (thresholding, mapping preferences to 0/1) are heuristic and ablated only lightly.

The Socratic Mind evaluation depends heavily on simulated student turns and LLM-as-judge scoring with modest calibration accuracy (0.66-0.7 test accuracy), on only ~1k preference pairs and 1,362 dialogues; effects in Table 9 are small relative to these noise sources.

Presentation issues: the 'Accuracy Value-guided' baseline in Table 2 is never introduced in the baseline descriptions; typos persist ('otain', 'Secrtion', 'potential' as 'potenial', 'based LLM'); and the distinction between PRM-guided and value-guided decoding (which Table 4 shows can differ substantially) deserves clearer exposition in the main text.

strengths: The paper is technically solid and unusually thorough in its empirical treatment: it includes standard deviations over 3 runs, discount-factor sweeps (Table 8), PRM noise-injection sensitivity studies (Tables 12-13), segmentation-strategy ablations (Table 9), KV-cache vs. text-chunk decoding comparisons (Tables 10-11), latency/memory benchmarks (Tables 6-7), a PPO-based baseline (Table 19), an explicit conflicting-objective subset (Table 20), cross-model evaluator validation (Appendix F.1), and a human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement (Appendix F.2).

The engineering contributions are sound and well-motivated: the continuing-hidden-state PRM-guided decoding addresses a real issue (re-encoding discontinuity and O(K(|x|N+NT)) re-encoding cost), and the gradient analysis in Appendix B.1 clearly explains why head-level routing reduces gradient interference relative to scalarized DPO.

The empirical findings are interesting and actionable, particularly Finding 7: reward verifiability determining whether test-time search or multi-objective training is the better investment is a useful, well-supported takeaway across the three domains.

The framework is coherent and general: a single pipeline covering verifiable (math), non-verifiable (human values), and interactive (tutoring) settings, with a unified PRM experiment (Figure 4) demonstrating cross-domain transfer of process supervision to non-verifiable dimensions.

Ethics and data treatment are handled responsibly, with IRB approval, de-identification, and clear data provenance described in Appendix B.2, and honest reporting of moderate judge-human agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.45).
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is a significant validity concern for the non-verifiable domains. In Human Values, results are scored by reward models trained on UltraFeedback-style preference data that is closely related to the training data; in Socratic Mind, evaluation scores come from PRMs trained with LLM-as-judge labels on the same dialogue distribution. Alignment 'gains' on these metrics may partly reflect optimizing toward the evaluator (Goodharting) rather than genuine improvement. Human validation is only provided for math engagement (100 samples, one dimension), so the central claims for helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness and tutoring engagement rest largely on self-referential metrics.

Methodological novelty is limited: multi-action-head DPO is essentially per-objective DPO heads on a shared backbone (a known decomposition, similar in spirit to MoE reward modeling and personalized soups), the PRM pipeline assembles existing techniques (Math-Shepherd rollouts, hindsight relabeling, LLM-as-judge calibration), and PRM-guided decoding is a variant of best-of-N/ARGS-style controlled decoding. No new theory is offered for when multi-head training should outperform scalarization.

Several headline gains are modest or mixed. In Math, MAH-DPO accuracy (0.7353) is within ~1 std of SFT (0.7300) and MODPO (0.7280); in Socratic Mind, MAH-DPO ensemble accuracy (0.6893) is below both Single-Head DPO (0.7040) and MODPO (0.7047), and combined MAH-DPO + Accuracy PRM (0.6659) underperforms Single-Head DPO alone, partially contradicting the 'synergy' claim (Finding 6).

Supervision quality in non-verifiable domains is weak and not fully propagated into conclusions: calibrated judges achieve only 75.8% (math engagement), 0.66 (Socratic engagement), and 0.7 (Socratic accuracy) test accuracy; Table 20 also reveals objectives are positively correlated in the main evaluation set, weakening the evidence for 'limited interference' in Table 1.

Test-time baselines are thin: despite citing ARGS, GenARM, PAD, and PARM, Table 4 compares only against unguided decoding with the authors' own decoding pipeline; no external reward-guided decoding baseline is reproduced, making the decoding contribution hard to situate.

Reproducibility is weakened by an empty code URL in the abstract ('Our code is available at:') and reliance on non-trivial, sparsely documented components (e.g., GPT-4o/Qwen-72B judge calibration sets of ~80-160 examples, judge ensembling mentioned but not specified).

The unified PRM is constructed by collapsing heterogeneous signals into a single binary classifier with ad hoc thresholds (e.g., math value scores > 0.85 -> 1), which sits awkwardly with the paper's stated motivation against collapsing multidimensional signals.

strengths: The paper covers an ambitious scope — verifiable rewards (math), non-verifiable preferences (helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness), and multi-turn tutoring — with a unified training-time (Multi-Action-Head DPO) and test-time (PRM-guided decoding) framework, plus a synergy study combining both.

Appendices contain substantial experimental detail and several genuinely useful ablations: segmentation-boundary robustness (Table 9), continuing-hidden-state vs. text-chunk decoding (Tables 10–11), injected PRM-noise sensitivity (Tables 12–13), a PPO-based baseline (MOPPO, Table 19), and a cross-model judge validation with GPT-4o plus a small human study (Appendix F).

The latency/throughput analysis (Tables 6–7) and the gradient-isolation discussion (Appendix B.1) are transparent about costs, and the continuing-hidden-state decoding trick is a practical contribution with a clear complexity argument.
The qualitative analysis of complementary vs. conflicting objectives (Appendix E.3) and the conflicting-subset experiment (Table 20) add some insight into when head separation helps.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. MAH-DPO reduces to per-objective linear output heads over a shared backbone with head-specific DPO losses — an incremental combination of known components (multi-objective reward modeling, e.g., Wang et al. 2024a mixture-of-experts reward models; MODPO; model soups). The PRM pipeline (hindsight relabeling, LLM-as-judge labeling, Bradley-Terry fallbacks) assembles standard techniques. The appendix 'gradient analysis' is trivial and provides no theory for why head isolation reduces interference, since backbone gradients are still an α-weighted sum exactly like scalarization.

Circular evaluation for non-verifiable objectives is the central evidential weakness. Helpfulness/honesty/truthfulness are measured by the very reward models used to construct preference pairs and to guide decoding, so gains in Tables 1(b), 4(b), and 5(b) may reflect reward-model exploitation rather than genuine alignment improvement. The engagement judge (Qwen2.5-70B) belongs to the same family as the preference-labeling model. The mitigation (GPT-4o cross-check and a 100-sample human study with only moderate agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.45) is too limited to rule this out for the main tables.

Controllability claims lack the decisive baseline: training-time scalarized DPO swept over α weights gives inference-time-controllable trade-offs at zero architectural cost (you can interpolate checkpoints or vary α at train time and pick per-deployment). The paper compares only fixed equal-weight MODPO/DPO Soup, so 'flexible user control' is not shown to be superior to trivial alternatives.

Key results are weak or contradicted by baselines: in Socratic Mind, MODPO and Single-Head DPO beat MAH-DPO on accuracy (Table 1c/18); in Math the accuracy gain over MODPO is within reported noise (0.7353 vs. 0.7280, stds ≈0.007). Moreover, in Table 16, simply adding an 'engaging' system prompt at test time achieves 0.9060 engagement — identical to the full MAH-DPO + PRM pipeline — suggesting much of the headline engagement gain comes from prompt engineering, not the proposed method.

Missing comparisons to established test-time alignment baselines (ARGS, GenARM, PARM, PAD, reward-augmented decoding) despite explicitly discussing them in related work; the PRM-guided decoding contribution is therefore not positioned against the strongest prior art.

Evaluation scale is small: MATH-500, 2k samples per Human Values dimension, 1,362 Socratic dialogues, 100 human-annotated samples; many reported differences are within one standard deviation. 'Finding 7' (verifiability determines training vs. test-time benefit) is a broad generalization drawn from essentially two settings.

Cross-domain generality is undermined by inconsistent setups: different base models (Qwen2.5-7B vs. Llama-3.1-8B), different judges (Qwen-72B, GPT-4o), different PRM architectures, and different hyperparameters per domain, so the 'unified framework' claim is more of a loosely connected set of per-domain pipelines.

Reproducibility: the abstract states 'Our code is available at:' with no URL provided; the unified PRM's thresholding (> 0.85 → 1) and normalization choices are ad hoc; the judgment-calibration procedures that determine all non-verifiable labels rely on prompts in Appendix H whose calibration quality is modest (0.66–0.81 test accuracy).

Presentation issues: the promise of a 'standardized PRM training pipeline' is diluted because the actual recipes differ substantially per domain (Case A/B/C), and the abstract/intro overstate the coherence and significance of the contributions relative to what the experiments support.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem — simultaneously aligning LLMs across verifiable rewards, non-verifiable subjective preferences, and multi-turn interactive settings — and provides a coherent framework (PRM training + Multi-Action-Head DPO + PRM-guided decoding) covering both training-time and test-time alignment.

Experimental coverage is unusually broad for this area: three domains (MATH, UltraFeedback-style human values, Socratic Mind tutoring), multiple baselines (MODPO, DPO Soup, Single-Head DPO, MOPPO), 3 seeds with standard deviations reported for all main tables, and many appendix-level ablations (segmentation robustness, PRM noise sensitivity, hidden-state vs. text-chunk decoding, discount factor sweeps, weight-sweep frontiers).

The evaluation-robustness analysis is commendable: cross-model validation with GPT-4o as an independent judge and a small human study (Table 22) partially mitigates concerns about LLM-judge circularity, at least for the Math engagement metric.

The KV-cache-carrying PRM-guided decoding is a thoughtful engineering contribution with clear complexity analysis (Appendix C.1) and a measured 4x speedup (Table 6), and the head-overhead analysis (Table 7) shows the multi-head design costs only ~13% latency.

Empirical findings are honestly framed, e.g., Finding 7 that verifiable rewards benefit more from test-time search while subjective rewards benefit more from training-time multi-objective optimization is a useful, well-supported insight; conflicts analysis (Table 20) and scaling to five heads (Table 21) probe the method's failure modes.
Reproducibility support is strong: extensive hyperparameters, data-construction recipes, judge calibration accuracies, system prompts, and a code release promise.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is a persistent concern beyond Math: in Human Values the metrics are scores from reward models, and in Socratic Mind engagement is judged by calibrated LLM-as-judges that also supply the training labels; models optimized against these signals may be partially reward-hacking the evaluator. The cross-model/human validation (Appendix F) covers only Math engagement, so the strongest risk of circularity remains unaddressed for the other domains.

Novelty is incremental. The multi-head DPO idea closely resembles existing multi-objective DPO variants (e.g., MODPO, multi-objective reward models with MoE), and PRM-guided decoding is well established; the main new elements are routing preference data to separate heads and the KV-cache continuation trick, neither of which is technically deep.

Several headline gains are modest or unfavorable. In Table 1, MAH-DPO's Math accuracy advantage over MODPO (0.7353 vs 0.7280) is within roughly one standard deviation, and on Socratic Mind the MAH-DPO ensemble accuracy (0.6893) is actually below Single-Head DPO (0.7040) and MODPO (0.7047). Statistical significance tests are not reported, so claims of 'most balanced performance' rest on small, sometimes inconsistent margins.

The largest Math gains come from test-time value/PRM guidance that relies on the pre-existing Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B rather than the paper's own PRM pipeline, making it unclear how much of the improvement is attributable to the proposed framework versus an off-the-shelf strong verifier.

Comparisons across tables are complicated by shifting baselines (e.g., Base accuracy 0.7107 in Table 1 vs 0.6853 under step-wise decoding in Table 4), which makes the 'synergy' claims (Table 5) harder to interpret without careful re-reading.

The tuning of engagement in Math is heavily prompt-driven (e.g., results 'w/ engaging prompt' in Table 16 are noticeably better), so part of the reported engagement improvement conflates the alignment method with simple system-prompt conditioning; a prompt-only ablation at equal compute would clarify this.

Human Values 'honesty/truthfulness/helpfulness' preference labels are themselves LLM-generated (UltraFeedback-style), adding an additional layer of label noise that the paper acknowledges only obliquely.
